title: Data Handling: Tables, Pictographs and Bar Graphs
seo_title: Tables, Pictographs and Bar Graphs Class 4 Worksheet with Answers (Maths Mela Chapter 14)
standard_code: Class 4, Maths Mela Chapter 14: Data Handling
standard_text: Data handling: collecting data, recording in tables, drawing and reading pictographs and bar graphs, and drawing conclusions (summary of NCERT Maths Mela Class 4)
meta_desc: Class 4 Data Handling worksheet (Maths Mela Chapter 14): tally tables, pictographs, bar graphs and comparing. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Read the scale on a bar graph carefully.
key_sub: In a pictograph, use the key.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A bar graph shows amounts as bars; read across from the top of the bar to the scale.
  • A pictograph key tells what each picture stands for.

Examples

Example

Bar for cricket reaches 35; for football 20.

35 − 20

Answer: 15 more chose cricket

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the bar between marks wronglyFind what each step on the scale is worth.
Ignoring the keyMultiply the pictures by the key.

faq.a: A graph that uses bars of different lengths to show amounts.
One picture can stand for many, so big numbers fit.

items.q: How many cars went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Car row has 3 groups of 5 and 4 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: How many lorries went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Lorry row has 4 groups of 5 and 3 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 3 = 23.

items.q: How many black cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Black row has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: Which row shows 11 cars?
items.e: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1. Look for 2 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is the Red row.

items.q: How many students chose swimming?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Swimming row has 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.

items.q: How many students are shown in the tally chart altogether?
items.e: Count each row: Football 18, Netball 9, Swimming 22, Cricket 11. Then add: 18 + 9 + 22 + 11 = 60 students.

items.q: How many robins were seen?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Robin row has 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.

items.q: What is the difference between the biggest and the smallest number of birds?
items.e: The biggest is Robin (22). The smallest is Blackbird (5). Difference means subtract: 22 − 5 = 17.

items.q: Which row shows 7 votes?
items.e: 7 = 5 + 2. Look for 1 group of 5 and 2 single marks. That is the Banana row.

items.q: How many votes are shown in the tally chart altogether?
items.e: Count each row: Apple 5, Banana 7, Grapes 22, Pear 18. Then add: 5 + 7 + 22 + 18 = 52 votes.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 3 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 3 = 18.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 5 groups of 5 and 2 more: 5 × 5 = 25, and 25 + 2 = 27.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 6 groups of 5 and 4 more: 6 × 5 = 30, and 30 + 4 = 34.
Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 8 groups of 5 and 1 more: 8 × 5 = 40, and 40 + 1 = 41.
23 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3, so look for 4 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is C. A shows 28 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 22 (one single mark is missing); D shows 24 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Mango?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Mango has 3 groups of 5 and 1 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 1 = 16.

items.q: Which fruit got the fewest votes?
items.e: Orange has the shortest tally: 1 group of 5 and 1 more, so 6 votes. Apple has 8, the next fewest.

items.q: How many more votes did Mango get than Watermelon?
items.e: Mango 16 (3 groups of 5 and 1 more). Watermelon 11. How many more means subtract: 16 − 11 = 5. (Counting each tally group as 4 makes Mango 13, and 13 − 11 = 2.)

items.q: Every student in 4B voted once. How many students are in 4B?
items.e: Find the Mango frequency first: 16. Then add all the rows: 8 + 13 + 16 + 6 + 11 = 54.

items.q: How many students have 2 pets?
items.e: Find the row for 2 pets. The frequency is 7, so 7 students have 2 pets. The 2 is the number of pets, not the number of students.

items.q: How many students have a cat?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 students. The Cat row has 2 circles: 2 × 2 = 4 students.
Look at the key: each star stands for 4 cakes. The Wed row has 2 stars and half a star: 2 × 4 = 8, and half of 4 is 2, so 8 + 2 = 10 cakes.

items.q: In this pictogram, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 4 students. Half a square is half of 4, which is 2 students, not 1.

items.q: How many cans did class 4A collect?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 10 cans. The 4A row has 4 circles and half a circle: 4 × 10 = 40, and half of 10 is 5, so 40 + 5 = 45 cans.
Every star stands for the same number, so the row with the most stars shows the most. The Autumn row has 5 stars: 5 × 4 = 20 votes.

items.q: How many votes did Green get?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 votes. The Green row has 1 square: 1 × 2 = 2 votes.

items.q: Each star stands for 4 books. Meera read 18 books. How many stars should be in her row?
items.e: 18 ÷ 4 = 4 remainder 2. 2 is half of 4, so draw 4 stars and half a star. Check: 4 × 4 + 2 = 18.
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 points. The Kestrel row has 5 stars and half a star: 5 × 10 = 50, and half of 10 is 5, so 50 + 5 = 55 points.

items.q: In this pictogram, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 10 books. Half a square is half of 10, which is 5 books, not 1.

items.q: Which row shows 10 shells?
items.e: 10 shells ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 2, so look for 2 and a half circles. The Rehan row has 2 circles and half a circle: 2 × 4 = 8, and half of 4 is 2, so 8 + 2 = 10 shells.

items.q: How many bald eagles were seen?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 birds. The Eagle row has 4 circles: 4 × 2 = 8 birds. (4 birds would mean each circle is 1.)
Every star stands for the same number, so the row with the most stars shows the most. The Basketball row has 6 stars: 6 × 2 = 12 students.

items.q: How many books did Anika read?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 books. The Anika row has 5 squares and half a square: 5 × 2 = 10, and half of 2 is 1, so 10 + 1 = 11 books. (6 books would mean each square is 1.)

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a circle stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole circle = 2 birds. Half a circle is half of 2, which is 1 bird. (Half a symbol is not always 1. It is half of the key.)
Half a star is 1. The Aditya row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 books.

items.q: Each circle stands for 2 students. 16 students chose football. How many circles should be in the Football row?
items.e: Count by 2s until you reach 16: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. That is 8 steps, so draw 8 circles. Check: 8 × 2 = 16. (Drawing 16 circles would mean each circle stands for 1.)

items.q: How many visitors came on Monday?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 5 visitors. The Mon row has 1 circle: 1 × 5 = 5 visitors. (1 visitor would mean each circle is 1.)
Each star = 5. 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so look for 3 stars. The Bike row has 3 stars: 3 × 5 = 15 students.

items.q: Which row shows the fewest laps?
items.e: Every square stands for the same number, so the row with the fewest squares shows the fewest. The Class 7 row has 1 square: 1 × 5 = 5 laps.

items.q: How many squares are in the Mr. Gill row?
items.e: Count the symbols in the row: 7 squares. Check with the key: 7 × 5 = 35. (The row does not have 35 squares. That would be the number of cans.)

items.q: What does the scale on this bar chart go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 2s.

items.q: How many cans did class 4D collect?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The 4D bar ends on the line for 15. So the answer is 15 cans.

items.q: How many students come by scooter to school?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The Scooter bar ends halfway between 10 and 20, so it shows 15. So the answer is 15 students.

items.q: How many votes did Banana get?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The Banana bar ends halfway between 4 and 6, so it shows 5. So the answer is 5 votes.

items.q: Which bar shows 10 shells?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Find 10 on the scale. The Nikhil bar ends on the line for 10.

items.q: How many sparrows were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The Sparrow bar ends halfway between 12 and 14, so it shows 13. So the answer is 13 birds.

items.q: How many points did Hawk House get?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The Hawk bar ends on the line for 30. So the answer is 30 points.

items.q: How many students have a hamster?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The Hamster bar ends halfway between 8 and 10, so it shows 9. So the answer is 9 students.

items.q: How many oak trees are in the park?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The Oak bar ends on the line for 70. So the answer is 70 trees.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar chart go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 10, 20, 30 … Each line is 10 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 10s.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 2s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many books did Arjun read?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Arjun ends on the line for 4. So the answer is 4 books.

items.q: How many ducks were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Duck ends halfway between 4 and 6, so it shows 5. So the answer is 5 birds.

items.q: Which bar shows 11 books?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Find 11 on the scale. The bar for Simran ends halfway between 10 and 12, so it shows 11.

items.q: Which bar shows the fewest birds?
items.e: The bar for Crow is the shortest one. The bar for Crow ends on the line for 4.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 5, 10, 15 … Each line is 5 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 5s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many visitors came on Thursday?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. The bar for Thu ends on the line for 10. So the answer is 10 visitors.

items.q: Which bar shows 10 students?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Find 10 on the scale. The bar for Car ends on the line for 10.

items.q: Which bar shows the most laps?
items.e: The bar for Class 7 is the tallest one. The bar for Class 7 ends on the line for 45.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 10, 20, 30 … Each line is 10 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 10s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many more books did Rehan read than Arjun?
items.e: Each circle stands for 2 books. Rehan: 3 × 2 + 1 = 7. Arjun: 1 × 2 = 2. How many more means find the difference: 7 − 2 = 5 books.

items.q: How many more herons than ducks were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Heron: 9. Duck: 2. How many more means find the difference: 9 − 2 = 7 birds.

items.q: How many more students come by car to school than take the bus?
items.e: Each square stands for 5 students. Car: 7 × 5 = 35. Bus: 5 × 5 = 25. How many more means find the difference: 35 − 25 = 10 students. (2 is the difference in symbols, not in students.)

items.q: How many more laps did the Class 5 students run than the Class 6 students?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Class 5: 40. Class 6: 20. How many more means find the difference: 40 − 20 = 20 laps. (4 is the difference in grid spaces, not in laps.)
Each star stands for 10 cans. Mr. Chen: 5 × 10 + 5 = 55. Mr. Gill: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. How many more means find the difference: 55 − 25 = 30 cans. (3 is the difference in symbols, not in cans.)

items.q: How many more visitors came on Monday than on Wednesday?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Mon: 70. Wed: 35. How many more means find the difference: 70 − 35 = 35 visitors.

items.q: How many fewer students chose basketball than swimming?
items.e: Each circle stands for 2 students. Swimming: 5 × 2 = 10. Basketball: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3. How many fewer means find the difference: 10 − 3 = 7 students.

items.q: How many fewer laps did the Class 7 students run than the Class 6 students?
items.e: Each square stands for 10 laps. Class 6: 4 × 10 + 5 = 45. Class 7: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. How many fewer means find the difference: 45 − 25 = 20 laps. (2 is the difference in symbols, not in laps.)

items.q: How many fewer cans did Mr. Gill’s class collect than Ms. Lee’s class?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Ms. Lee: 55. Mr. Gill: 35. How many fewer means find the difference: 55 − 35 = 20 cans. (2 is the difference in grid spaces, not in cans.)
Each star stands for 5 visitors. Wed: 6 × 5 = 30. Thu: 4 × 5 = 20. Altogether means add: 30 + 20 = 50 visitors.

items.q: Neha will draw a pictograph of these votes: 40, 25, 35 and 50. She wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as she can. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so a key of 5 gives whole symbols: 8, 5, 7 and 10. A key of 10 or 2 would need half symbols for 25 and 35. A key of 1 needs 150 symbols.

items.q: Varun will draw a pictograph of 60, 90, 40 and 70 students. He wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as he can. Which key should he use?
items.e: Every number is a multiple of 10, so a key of 10 gives whole symbols: 6, 9, 4 and 7 (26 symbols). A key of 5 also works, but it needs twice as many symbols (52).

items.q: Varun will draw a column graph of 12, 18, 6 and 14 votes. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and he wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 1s needs 18 gridlines, which is too many. Counting in 2s needs 9 gridlines (2 to 18), and every number is even, so every column ends on a line. In 5s or 10s, 12, 18, 6 and 14 would end between lines.

items.q: Tara will draw a column graph of 35, 50, 20 and 45 tickets. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and she wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 5s needs 10 gridlines (5 to 50), and every number is in the 5 times table. 1s or 2s need far too many lines (50 or 25). In 10s, 35 and 45 would end halfway between lines.

items.q: Raffle tickets sold (frequency table): 4A 45, 4B 70, 4C 30, 4D 55. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 10s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 20, Tue 30, Wed 15, Thu 25. Which pictograph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 10). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. How many tickets should the missing 4C column show?
items.e: Read the 4C row of the pictograph. Each circle = 10 tickets. The 4C row has 3 circles and half a circle: 3 × 10 = 30, and half of 10 is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35 tickets. Draw the 4C column up to 35.
Read the Tara row of the pictograph. Each star = 2 books. The Tara row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 books. Draw the Tara column up to 9.

items.q: How many students read 3 books?
items.e: Each dot is one student. Count the dots above 3: there are 5. (3 is the number of books, not the number of students.)

items.q: Class 4 want to collect 200 cans for charity. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: Step 1: cans so far: 40 + 25 + 55 + 30 = 150. Step 2: 200 − 150 = 50. (Reading the 4B bar as 20 or 30 gives a wrong total.)
Each star = 4 books, so half a star = 2. Kavya: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. Tara: 2 × 4 + 2 = 10. Altogether means add: 14 + 10 = 24.

items.q: How many more cakes were sold on Friday than on Monday?
items.e: Each circle = 10 cakes, so half a circle = 5. Friday: 5 × 10 = 50. Monday: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. How many more means subtract: 50 − 25 = 25.

items.q: How many tickets were sold altogether?
items.e: Add all four cells: 46 + 38 = 84 on Thursday and 62 + 54 = 116 on Friday. 84 + 116 = 200.

items.q: How many more cars went past than buses and lorries together?
items.e: Cars: 4 groups of 5 and 3 more = 23. Buses and lorries together: 7 + 9 = 16. Difference: 23 − 16 = 7.

items.q: The chart shows all 30 days of April. The class played outside at lunchtime on every day that was not rainy. On how many days did they play outside?
items.e: Step 1: the Rainy bar ends on the line for 8, so 8 days were rainy. Step 2: 30 − 8 = 22 days. Check: 12 + 7 + 3 = 22.

items.q: The journey to the seaside is 80 km. How much further did the car still have to go at 10:30?
items.e: At 10:30 the point is on the line for 30, so the car had travelled 30 km. Still to go: 80 − 30 = 50 km.

items.q: How much warmer was the warmest time of the day than 09:00?
items.e: The warmest point is 16 °C at 13:00. At 09:00 it was 7 °C. Difference: 16 − 7 = 9 °C.

items.q: How many students chose kabaddi?
items.e: The scale counts by 5s. The kabaddi bar ends on the line for 15. (3 counts the grid spaces as 1 each.)

items.q: How many more students chose football than kabaddi?
items.e: Football 35, kabaddi 15. How many more means subtract: 35 − 15 = 20. (4 is the difference in grid spaces, and 50 adds the two bars.)

items.q: The school will start clubs for the two most popular sports. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest bars are football (35) and basketball (30). Hockey is 25, the third tallest.

items.q: The students who chose basketball make teams of 5 for a lunch tournament. How many teams do they make?
items.e: Basketball ends on 30. 30 ÷ 5 = 6 teams. (7 teams comes from using the football bar, 35. 150 multiplies instead of dividing.)

items.q: Every student chose one sport. How many students took part in the survey?
Every Class 4 student voted once. How many students are in Class 4?
items.e: Read every column: 25 + 15 + 30 + 20 + 10 = 100. (20 counts grid spaces: 5 + 3 + 6 + 4 + 2.)

items.q: Rehan says, “Twice as many students chose AFL as chose swimming.” Is he right?
c: No. AFL got 5 and swimming got 2.
No. Twice 10 is 20, but AFL got 25.
Yes. AFL is the most popular sport.
Yes. AFL got 25 and swimming got 10.
items.e: Swimming 10, AFL 25. Twice 10 is 20, and 25 is more than 20, so he is not right. (5 and 2 are grid spaces, not students.)

items.q: How many students come to school by car?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 students. The Car row has 8 circles: 8 × 10 = 80. (8 reads each circle as 1 student.)

items.q: How many more students come by car than walk?
items.e: Car: 8 circles = 80. Walk: 4 circles and half a circle = 40 + 5 = 45. 80 − 45 = 35. (Leaving out the half circle gives 80 − 40 = 40.)

items.q: How many students walk, ride a bike or ride a scooter?
items.e: Walk 45, Bike 20, Scooter 15 (1 circle and half a circle). 45 + 20 + 15 = 80. (Leaving out the half circles gives 40 + 20 + 10 = 70. 8 counts the circles.)

items.q: Next term, 20 students who come by car will walk instead. What should the Walk row show then?
items.e: Walk now: 45. 45 + 20 = 65 students. 65 = 60 + 5: 6 circles for 60 and half a circle for 5.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the pictograph?
c: More students come by car than walk and ride a scooter together.
The bus is the least common way to travel.
No students come to school by train.
items.e: Car 80. Walk and scooter: 45 + 15 = 60. 80 is more, so this is supported. Walking (45) is not most of the 195 students. Train was not in the survey, so we cannot tell. Scooter (15) is the least common.
